sets.name: C2 Philosophy & Ethics
sets.description: Abstract thought, morality, and philosophical concepts

words.definition: The branch of philosophy studying knowledge
words.example: Epistemology asks: what can we know?

words.definition: The study of reality and existence
words.example: Metaphysics explores the nature of being.

words.definition: The study of what exists
words.example: Ontology examines the categories of being.

words.definition: The belief in selfless concern for others
words.example: His altruism led him to volunteer.

words.definition: The belief that life has no meaning
words.example: Nihilism rejects all moral principles.

words.definition: The theory that knowledge comes from experience
words.example: Empiricism relies on observation and experiment.

words.definition: The belief that all events are caused by prior events
words.example: Determinism leaves no room for free will.

words.definition: A practical approach to problems and ideas
words.example: Pragmatism values what works in practice.

words.definition: To think deeply and at length about something
words.example: She contemplated the meaning of existence.

words.definition: To assume the existence or truth of something
words.example: The theory postulates a parallel universe.

words.definition: Existing as a natural part of something
words.example: There are inherent contradictions in the argument.

words.definition: Belonging naturally; essential
words.example: Happiness has intrinsic value.

words.definition: The right to govern yourself or make your own decisions
words.example: Individual autonomy is a key human right.

words.definition: The art of investigating truths through discussion
words.example: Plato's dialogues use the dialectic method.

words.definition: Designed to be useful rather than attractive
words.example: Mill's utilitarian ethics maximize happiness.

words.definition: Relating to existence and individual experience
words.example: Climate change poses an existential threat.

words.definition: A statement that seems contradictory but may be true
words.example: It's a paradox that more choice can mean less happiness.

words.definition: Based on personal feelings rather than facts
words.example: Beauty is subjective.

words.definition: Based on facts, not personal feelings
words.example: We need an objective assessment.

words.definition: The theory that the morality of an action depends on its outcome
words.example: Consequentialism judges actions by their results.

sets.name: C2 Law & Justice
sets.description: Legal systems, court proceedings, and justice

words.definition: The official power to make legal decisions
words.example: This case falls under federal jurisdiction.

words.definition: Laws enacted by a governing body
words.example: The new legislation takes effect next month.

words.definition: The process of taking legal action
words.example: The company faces litigation over patent infringement.

words.definition: A formal statement given in court
words.example: The witness gave testimony under oath.

words.definition: The decision of a jury or judge
words.example: The jury returned a guilty verdict.

words.definition: A written law passed by a legislative body
words.example: The statute was enacted in 1990.

words.definition: A previous case that guides future legal decisions
words.example: This ruling sets a legal precedent.

words.definition: The person who brings a case against another in court
words.example: The plaintiff filed a lawsuit.

words.definition: A person accused or sued in court
words.example: The defendant pleaded not guilty.

words.definition: To declare someone not guilty
words.example: The jury acquitted the accused.

words.definition: To find someone guilty of a crime
words.example: He was convicted of fraud.

words.definition: To make a formal judgment about a dispute
words.example: The court adjudicated the claim.

words.definition: A period of supervised behavior instead of prison
words.example: He was sentenced to two years of probation.

words.definition: A formal charge of a serious crime
words.example: The grand jury issued an indictment.

words.definition: A wrongful act leading to civil legal liability
words.example: Defamation is a common tort.

words.definition: Required or allowed by law
words.example: The company has statutory obligations.

words.definition: Relating to courts of law
words.example: The judicial system must be independent.

words.definition: Using a neutral person to settle a dispute outside court
words.example: They resolved the conflict through arbitration.

words.definition: The state of being legally responsible
words.example: The company admitted liability for the accident.

words.definition: An official pardon for political offenses
words.example: The government granted amnesty to political prisoners.

sets.name: C2 Idioms & Expressions
sets.description: Advanced idiomatic expressions and figurative language

words.definition: To initiate conversation in a social situation
words.example: A joke can help break the ice at parties.

words.word: hit the nail on the head
words.definition: To describe exactly what is causing a situation
words.example: You hit the nail on the head with that analysis.

words.definition: To endure a painful situation with courage
words.example: I had to bite the bullet and tell the truth.

words.definition: To work late into the night
words.example: She burned the midnight oil to finish her thesis.

words.definition: Feeling ill or unwell
words.example: I'm feeling a bit under the weather today.

words.word: the ball is in your court
words.definition: It's your turn to make a decision
words.example: I've made my offer — the ball is in your court.

words.word: cost an arm and a leg
words.definition: To be very expensive
words.example: That designer bag costs an arm and a leg.

words.definition: Very rarely
words.example: I only see her once in a blue moon.

words.definition: To reveal a secret
words.example: Come on, spill the beans — what happened?

words.definition: Something that seems bad but turns out to be good
words.example: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.

words.definition: To avoid talking about the main topic
words.example: Stop beating around the bush and tell me.

words.word: let the cat out of the bag
words.definition: To accidentally reveal a secret
words.example: He let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.

words.definition: In a risky or dangerous situation
words.example: He's on thin ice after being late three times.

words.definition: A small part of a much bigger problem
words.example: These complaints are just the tip of the iceberg.

words.definition: Making a wrong assumption about something
words.example: If you think I did it, you're barking up the wrong tree.

words.definition: Something very easy to do
words.example: The exam was a piece of cake.

words.definition: To destroy a relationship or possibility of return
words.example: Don't burn bridges — you might need that contact later.

words.definition: To do something in the easiest or cheapest way
words.example: They cut corners on safety to save money.

words.definition: To become difficult to control
words.example: The situation got out of hand quickly.

words.definition: To make more effort than expected
words.example: She always goes the extra mile for her clients.
